idiom_name: Node Permission Model at runtime, # private fields plus branded capability types at compile time
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds a compile-time layer over JavaScript's runtime, and both halves matter here. The type layer expresses authority in signatures: Pick<T, ...> and Readonly<T> hand a component a narrowed view, and a branded or unique-symbol capability token makes the right to call privileged methods unforgeable in the type system, so the classic rights-table object is replaced by the shape of the value a component receives. The runtime layer is JavaScript's and the platform's: # private fields are enforced by the language ('hard privacy', supported since TypeScript 3.8 and ES2022) rather than by the private modifier, which disappears in the emitted code, and Node's Permission Model (--permission with --allow-fs-read, --allow-child-process and the irreversible process.permission.drop()) bounds what the process may do at all. Framework guards (NestJS CanActivate, Express middleware, OAuth scopes on the token) decide per request above that. The classic form is justified where entitlements are runtime data, and the caveat is structural: types are erased, so a type must never be the only check.
pitfalls: Types are erased: branded tokens, readonly views and Pick-shaped interfaces can be forged from JavaScript or defeated with a cast, so pair them with a runtime check (private state, a closed module, a policy in the framework) at the point that matters.

private is not #: the TypeScript modifier leaves the property reachable at runtime, while # private fields are enforced by the language - and even they do not stop code inside the same class from acting with the instance's authority.

A guard at the edge does not cover every caller: a queue consumer, a scheduled job or an internal service can call the same privileged code without passing the route guard, so the check belongs where the resource is touched, not only where the request enters.
